explanations.explanation: That's the one. David says, "For I have walked with integrity; I have trusted in the LORD without wavering." He doesn't hand over a trophy list. He points to how he has walked. Plain and steady, and I respect that.

Battles are a big deal for a king, so I get why this one tempts a baker. But David never mentions a single battle in this song. His reason is right there in the first verse: "For I have walked with integrity…" If it were me, I'd show up with a whole highlight reel.

David does bring up the LORD's altar later in the song, so this one has a little something going for it. But offerings aren't his reason in verse 1. He says, "For I have walked with integrity…" Walking, not giving, is what he points to.

True! David says, "I have trusted in the LORD without wavering." Without wavering means he kept leaning on the LORD, not just on the easy days. I wobble when I carry a full tray of hot cookies across the kitchen, so that kind of steady is impressive to me.

This one is actually true. Right in verse 1, David says, "I have trusted in the LORD without wavering." He says it plainly and he says it to the LORD. So the statement on the card matches the text exactly.

Close, but David asks for more than that. He says, "Test me, O LORD, and try me; examine my heart and mind." So the heart is right in the request, not left alone. He's inviting the LORD to look at the inside, not just the outside.
Right, it's false. David says, "Test me, O LORD, and try me; examine my heart and mind." He doesn't keep his heart off the table. He holds nothing back, and that takes nerve.

Yes, friend. David says, "For Your loving devotion is before my eyes, and I have walked in Your truth." What he keeps in view is the LORD's loving devotion. His eyes are on God's love, not on himself.

I can see why this would sound right, since David talks about his walk all through the song. But the thing before his eyes is something else. Verse 3 says, "For Your loving devotion is before my eyes…" He's looking at the LORD's love, not his own résumé.

David does talk about other people's company in the next verses, so this one has some pull. But verse 3 is about what he's looking at, and that's "Your loving devotion." The text doesn't say he's watching anybody's faults. His eyes are on the LORD's love.

That's it. David says, "I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites." Deceitful men are the ones he doesn't sit with. Notice that he says it about where he sits, which is a pretty ordinary thing, like picking a seat.

Proud men are a fair guess, but they aren't in this verse. David says, "I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites." The word is deceitful. Pay attention to the exact words and you'll catch these every time.

Foolish men don't show up in this verse. David says, "I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites." Deceitful is the word, and hypocrites come right after it. The song stays with those two.

Yes, hates. David says, "I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked." It's a strong word, and he says it out loud to the LORD. His seat choice matches it: he refuses to sit with the wicked.
Leads doesn't fit what David says. He says, "I hate the mob of evildoers…" He isn't at the front of that crowd. He's staying away from it.

Fears is an understandable guess, since a mob sounds scary. But the word David uses is hate: "I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked." The text doesn't say he's afraid of them. It says he refuses to sit with them.

explanations.answer: So he can go about the LORD's altar
explanations.explanation: Right on. David says, "I wash my hands in innocence that I may go about Your altar, O LORD." The washing is for going about the LORD's altar. He's getting ready to be in the LORD's presence.

explanations.answer: So he can sit with the elders
explanations.explanation: Elders don't show up in this song at all. David says he washes his hands "that I may go about Your altar, O LORD." The altar is the reason. Sitting is something he says he refuses to do with the wicked, not the reason for his washing.

explanations.answer: So he can stand before the people
explanations.explanation: Standing before the people sounds like something a king would do, but that isn't what David says. He says, "I wash my hands in innocence that I may go about Your altar, O LORD." The altar is where his washing is headed.

Not quite. David says he'll go about the altar "to raise my voice in thanksgiving and declare all Your wonderful works." His voice goes up in thanksgiving, not complaint. I've been known to complain at my oven, but that's not what David plans here.

Correct, it's false. David says he'll go about the altar "to raise my voice in thanksgiving and declare all Your wonderful works." Thanksgiving is what he plans to raise his voice for. He also plans to declare the LORD's wonderful works.

explanations.answer: The house where the LORD dwells
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "O LORD, I love the house where You dwell, the place where Your glory resides." He loves the house where the LORD dwells. I'll tell you, my bakery feels like home to me, but David is talking about something even bigger.

David is a king, so a palace is a natural guess. But the text never mentions one in this song. He says, "O LORD, I love the house where You dwell, the place where Your glory resides." The love goes to the LORD's house.

explanations.answer: The hills where he grew up
explanations.explanation: Hills where he grew up would be a sweet answer, but the song doesn't say that. What David loves is in verse 8: "the house where You dwell, the place where Your glory resides." It's the LORD's house, and nothing in the text points to his childhood home.

explanations.answer: Take his soul away with sinners
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the request. David says, "Do not take my soul away with sinners, or my life with men of bloodshed." He asks the LORD not to take his soul away with them. It's a plain request from the heart.
Hiding His face is a different prayer. It shows up in other psalms, but it's not in this one. Here David says, "Do not take my soul away with sinners, or my life with men of bloodshed."

The wilderness doesn't appear anywhere in this song. David's request is in verse 9: "Do not take my soul away with sinners, or my life with men of bloodshed." It's about being taken away with sinners, not being left somewhere.

True. David says of them, "in whose hands are wicked schemes, whose right hands are full of bribes." Wicked schemes are in their hands. Their right hands carry bribes too. Compare that to David washing his own hands in verse 6.

This one is true, actually. David says the men of bloodshed are "in whose hands are wicked schemes, whose right hands are full of bribes." So wicked schemes are in their hands, just as the card says. It's a picture of hands full of the wrong things.

explanations.answer: To redeem him and be merciful
explanations.explanation: That's the one. David says, "But I will walk with integrity; redeem me and be merciful to me." He ends his promise with a request for mercy. I think that's a humble way to follow up a strong claim.
Riches don't come up in this song. Right after "But I will walk with integrity," David says, "redeem me and be merciful to me." Redeem and mercy are the two things he asks for.
A great name isn't what he asks for here. Verse 11 says, "But I will walk with integrity; redeem me and be merciful to me." He asks to be redeemed and shown mercy, and nothing about his name.

Yes, bless. David closes with, "My feet stand on level ground; in the congregations I will bless the LORD." He plans to bless the LORD in the congregations, with other people around. It's a good way to end a song.
Question doesn't fit how David ends the song. He says, "in the congregations I will bless the LORD." The word is bless. His last line is praise, not questions.

Test shows up earlier in the song, which is why it might ring a bell. But there, David asks the LORD to test him: "Test me, O LORD, and try me…" (Psalm 26:2). In the last verse, the word is bless: "in the congregations I will bless the LORD."
